publication_type: Topic-level evidence synthesis combining experimental classroom studies, large-scale field monitoring, thermal-comfort field studies, IoT deployment papers, and standards-oriented guidance.
country_and_climate: The evidence covers Türkiye, the northeastern United States, Spain, Malta, and broader international classroom reviews. Climate contexts include Mediterranean, temperate, and heat-stressed school buildings, which matters because naturally ventilated classrooms, top floors, and buildings with little or no mechanical cooling show stronger overheating and wider adaptive responses.
objective_and_research_question: The common goal is to quantify classroom temperature and relative humidity continuously, relate those measurements to thermal comfort and student outcomes, and use the results to guide ventilation, cooling, and operations. For an IoT classroom system, the key question is how to measure temperature and humidity cheaply but credibly, while recognizing that thermal comfort itself is a derived construct that also depends on radiant temperature, air speed, clothing, metabolism, adaptation, and occupant perception.
study_design: The topic relies on observational field studies, experimental or quasi-experimental classroom studies, district-scale longitudinal sensor networks, and IoT system implementation papers. Many studies pair objective measurements with surveys or comfort models such as PMV/PPD or adaptive comfort frameworks.
educational_context: The evidence spans primary, secondary, and university classrooms with naturally ventilated, mixed-mode, and mechanically conditioned rooms. The operational problems are consistent across settings: overheating on upper floors, uneven conditions between classrooms in the same building, and comfort-energy trade-offs when ventilation is increased without adequate cooling or shading.
sample_and_duration: Large-scale evidence includes minute-level temperature monitoring from more than 3,600 classrooms in 125 Boston school buildings during the 2023 hot season. Other field studies follow classrooms over weeks, seasons, or a full academic year, while experimental studies use shorter controlled periods to link thermal conditions with comfort and learning performance.
environmental_variables: Core variables are air temperature in degrees Celsius and relative humidity in percent. For full comfort assessment, the literature also highlights mean radiant temperature, operative temperature, air speed, outdoor conditions, occupancy, solar exposure, and sometimes PMV/PPD, adaptive comfort metrics, and overheating exposure metrics that capture intensity, frequency, and duration rather than simple daily averages.
outdoor_conditions_and_baseline: Outdoor temperature, humidity, solar gains, and building orientation strongly shape indoor thermal loads, especially in naturally ventilated and lightly conditioned classrooms. Outdoor conditions are also needed for adaptive comfort interpretation, because acceptable indoor temperature ranges widen when occupants can adapt and outdoor conditions are warmer.
occupancy_and_activity: Classrooms are mostly sedentary spaces, but occupancy density, lesson duration, computer use, vocal activity, and the number of bodies in the room still add internal heat and moisture loads. Class schedules matter because start-of-day conditions, occupancy peaks, and post-break recovery periods can differ sharply within the same room.
ventilation_and_filtration_operation: Thermal comfort outcomes depend on how ventilation is delivered and whether cooling is available. Natural ventilation can improve perceived freshness but may raise or lower temperature depending on season and outdoor conditions; central AC, window AC, and no-AC classrooms show clearly different heat exposure profiles. Filtration has little direct thermal benefit unless coupled with fans that alter air movement and perceived comfort.
spatial_granularity: Thermal conditions vary substantially within buildings and even within single classrooms, so one centrally placed node is a minimum, not a full map. Boston district data showed average intra-building temperature variation of 2.3 degrees Celsius and a maximum of 14.3 degrees Celsius, demonstrating that school-level or even building-level averages can mask room-level discomfort and inequity.
sensor_specification: For low-cost IoT monitoring of temperature and humidity, a practical core sensor is the Sensirion SHT45: digital I2C interface, operating range of 0 to 100 percent RH and minus 40 to 125 degrees Celsius, typical accuracy around plus or minus 1 percent RH and plus or minus 0.1 degrees Celsius, and strong low-power performance. For full research-grade thermal comfort, add sensors or instruments for mean radiant temperature and air speed because temperature and humidity alone cannot fully reproduce PMV/PPD or local discomfort metrics.
calibration_and_qaqc: Temperature and humidity nodes should be co-located before deployment, checked again after field use, and inspected for enclosure-induced self-heating or moisture lag. QA/QC should include time synchronization, removal of startup transients, shielding from direct sun, and confirmation that the sensor is not mounted in a stagnant enclosure or near a hot regulator, display, or Wi-Fi radio.
acquisition_and_data_quality: Continuous logging at 1 to 5 minute intervals is suitable for school operations, while 30 to 60 second sampling helps research on fast indoor dynamics and exposure metrics. Data cleaning should flag implausible steps, flat lines, sensor warm-up periods, and abrupt changes caused by relocation or unplugging. Missing data and uptime should be reported explicitly because exposure metrics are sensitive to gaps on the hottest days.
sensor_lifecycle: [uncertain] Temperature and humidity sensors are generally long-lived and stable, but classroom reliability still depends on dust, condensation, cleaning practices, enclosure design, and the thermal behavior of the host electronics. In low-cost nodes, wiring faults, power interruptions, or condensation events often create more field problems than intrinsic sensor wear.
recommended_sensor_by_variable: For temperature and relative humidity, recommend a digital CMOS sensor class with documented field use and low drift, such as the SHT45. If the aim is true thermal comfort rather than simple screening, also recommend at least one radiant-temperature channel and, where drafts matter, an air-speed measurement path. For a low-cost TCC prototype, start with T and RH plus occupant surveys, and only add globe temperature or air-speed modules where the research question requires standards-grade comfort modeling.
useful_output_and_units: Useful outputs are air temperature in degrees Celsius, relative humidity in percent, derived absolute humidity or dew point when needed, occupied-period mean and peak temperature, overheating duration, percent of time outside comfort bands, and if enough variables are available, operative temperature and comfort-classification outputs.
direct_measurement_or_proxy: Air temperature and relative humidity are direct physical measurements. Thermal comfort is not directly measured by the sensor; it is inferred through comfort models or captured subjectively with occupant votes. A node that measures only temperature and humidity provides a useful proxy for screening comfort risk but not a complete comfort diagnosis.
measurement_principle_and_selectivity: Modern classroom T/RH nodes typically use integrated CMOS humidity and temperature sensors with digital preprocessing and humidity compensation. These sensors are selective and mature for T/RH, but they do not directly sense radiant asymmetry, air movement, or personal adaptation, which are often the missing pieces in classroom comfort interpretation.
useful_range_and_real_performance: A practical classroom monitoring range is about 15 to 35 degrees Celsius and 20 to 80 percent RH, though sensors should cover wider extremes to avoid clipping during storage or severe weather. Experimental evidence from Kirkil 2025 suggests that maintaining classrooms around 20 to 22 degrees Celsius was associated with better learning performance in that study, while district-scale monitoring shows that substantial overheating still occurs in schools with weak cooling provision.
operating_regime: Continuous operation is preferred, with 1 minute sampling for exposure analytics and 5 minute sampling acceptable for dashboarding and alerts. A short warm-up period and stable airflow around the sensing element are important. For dense deployments, mains-powered nodes are easier to maintain than battery nodes once communication, display, and uptime requirements are considered.
interferences_and_confounders: Major confounders are direct solar radiation, self-heating from the MCU or power regulation, placement near windows, doors, ducts, or occupants, condensation, and poor enclosure ventilation. Relative humidity readings are also temperature-dependent in practice, so a thermally biased node often produces both wrong temperature and misleading humidity.
affordable_validation_protocol: A low-cost protocol is to co-locate all classroom nodes with one better-characterized temperature and humidity reference in a shaded indoor location for 24 to 72 hours across cool and warm conditions, then repeat a shorter post-deployment check. During installation, record room orientation, height, distance from windows and HVAC, and any shielding. If comfort modeling is required, add a black-globe or radiant-temperature measurement for a subset of rooms to calibrate how much information the simpler nodes miss.
validation_metrics: Recommended metrics are temperature bias in degrees Celsius, RH bias in percent RH, MAE, RMSE, inter-sensor agreement, drift between pre- and post-checks, uptime, and missing-data fraction. For comfort analytics, also report how often simplified T/RH-based alerts agree with a fuller comfort assessment that includes radiant temperature, air speed, and occupant feedback.
installation_and_enclosure: Install the node in the occupied zone, typically near seated head height, with free airflow and protection from direct solar gain. Keep it away from windows, doors, supply vents, radiators, projectors, and electronics that radiate heat. Use a vented enclosure and, if the controller runs warm, physically separate the sensing head from the main PCB or use stand-offs and openings that prevent heat buildup.
hardware_integration: SHT45-class sensors integrate easily over I2C with ESP32-class MCUs and have low power demand, making them suitable for classroom nodes with local storage and Wi-Fi or LoRa uplinks. For richer comfort nodes, add optional globe-temperature and air-speed channels, but expect higher power use, more wiring complexity, and greater calibration burden.
total_implementation_cost: [uncertain] As of August 11, 2026, DigiKey lists the SHT45 around USD 5.76 in low quantity. A simple classroom T/RH node with ESP32, SHT45, enclosure, PCB, power supply, and mounting hardware is typically about USD 10 to USD 25 per room, while a fuller comfort node with radiant-temperature and airflow instrumentation can move into the roughly USD 35 to USD 120 range before labor and software.
evidence_maturity: Evidence maturity is high for low-cost continuous temperature and humidity measurement, moderate for using dense classroom monitoring to reveal overheating inequity, and moderate for comfort inference from simplified sensor sets. Evidence is weaker whenever a study tries to infer full thermal comfort from temperature and humidity alone without radiant temperature, air speed, and subjective responses.
variable_specific_cautions: Temperature and humidity are necessary but not sufficient for thermal comfort. Avoid self-heating, sunlit walls, and HVAC drafts. RH should not be interpreted without temperature context. Simple thresholds are useful for screening, but naturally ventilated classrooms often show adaptive behavior that can make fixed narrow setpoints misleading.
system_architecture: A suitable architecture is classroom node to gateway or campus network to time-series storage to dashboards that summarize occupied-period temperature, RH, and overheating metrics. At scale, the dashboard should support room, building, floor, and district views so facilities teams can identify top-floor overheating, weak AC performance, and rooms that consistently fall outside operational comfort bands.
connectivity_and_protocols: Wi-Fi plus MQTT or HTTPS is usually the fastest route for pilot deployments. LoRaWAN is attractive for dense retrofits with sparse power and network access. The protocol decision should reflect school IT policy, expected message frequency, and whether the program needs near-real-time alerts or mainly daily analytics.
interoperability_and_data_model: Each record should include timestamp, room ID, sensor ID, air temperature, RH, occupancy flag if available, and QA status. Interoperability is better when room metadata includes floor, orientation, HVAC type, and whether the room has central AC, window AC, or no AC, because these attributes materially improve later analysis and actionability.
cybersecurity_privacy_and_ethics: Temperature and humidity monitoring carries little direct privacy risk, but room-level heat maps can expose inequities between classes or schools and can still be misused for staff performance narratives. Use authenticated devices and encrypted transport, restrict access to room-level dashboards to operational roles, and frame the system as environmental monitoring rather than behavioral surveillance.
analytical_methods: Useful methods include time-series summaries by occupied period, overheating metrics, comparison across HVAC categories, floor-level and orientation-level stratification, PMV or adaptive comfort calculations when enough variables are available, and mixed objective-subjective analysis that compares sensor outputs with occupant comfort votes.
derived_index_or_model: Derived measures include dew point, apparent moisture patterns, occupied-period overheating duration, adaptive comfort classification, and if the instrument set is complete enough, PMV/PPD or operative temperature. The Boston heat paper also highlights the value of exposure metrics that combine intensity, frequency, and duration instead of relying only on daily mean temperature.
decision_rules_and_standards: A two-layer rule set is best. For rigorous comfort studies, apply ASHRAE 55 or EN 16798-style methods using operative temperature and the relevant contextual variables. For school operations dashboards, use simple screening alerts such as persistent occupied temperatures below about 20 degrees Celsius in cool periods or above about 26 degrees Celsius in warm periods, plus RH excursions above about 60 percent, while recognizing that naturally ventilated classrooms may accept broader adaptive ranges.
intervention_and_automation: Operational actions include shading, purge ventilation at appropriate times, HVAC schedule adjustment, fan-speed or setpoint tuning, room reassignment during extreme heat, and capital prioritization for classrooms with chronic overheating. Automation can escalate from traffic-light dashboards to rule-based HVAC or window-control logic, but the control design should avoid solving temperature problems by sacrificing ventilation quality.
environmental_outcomes: Continuous monitoring reveals overheating hotspots, floor-to-floor inequity, and the thermal cost of inadequate cooling capacity. It also helps distinguish transient discomfort from chronic building performance problems and supports evidence-based prioritization of cooling, shading, and envelope interventions.
health_and_learning_outcomes: The literature consistently treats thermal comfort as relevant to concentration, satisfaction, and learning conditions. In Kirkil 2025, maintaining classrooms around 20 to 22 degrees Celsius was identified as important for academic performance in that experiment. Large-scale heat monitoring further shows that students in classrooms without effective AC face substantially higher exposure to extreme heat, which is a clear resilience and equity concern.
objective_subjective_integration: Combining sensors with quick thermal sensation or satisfaction surveys is strongly recommended because students often adapt differently than predicted by generic adult-centered models. Studies in educational buildings report that subjective responses can reveal broader acceptable ranges or different preferred temperatures than standard models suggest.
quantitative_results: Key quantitative findings include: the Boston district study monitored minute-level temperature data from over 3,600 classrooms in 125 buildings; average intra-building temperature variation was 2.3 degrees Celsius, with a maximum of 14.3 degrees Celsius; and on hot days classrooms exceeded extreme-caution thresholds by 0.1 percent, 1.1 percent, and 8.4 percent in schools with central AC, window AC, and no AC, respectively. Kirkil 2025 also reported that 20 to 22 degrees Celsius was the most favorable range in that learning-performance experiment.
feasibility_and_acceptance: Temperature and humidity monitoring is one of the most feasible parts of a classroom IoT stack because sensors are cheap, compact, and mature. Acceptance is typically high when the output is easy to understand and clearly linked to building improvements rather than individual blame. The main challenge is not sensing cost but disciplined installation, metadata capture, and using the data to trigger real facilities action.
validity_and_limitations: A T/RH-only node does not fully measure thermal comfort, and room-level conditions can vary enough that one sensor may not represent every desk. Seasonal adaptation, clothing, radiant asymmetry, and airflow remain important unmeasured factors in many low-cost deployments. Results also depend strongly on building type, orientation, and climate, so threshold transfer should be done cautiously.
contribution_and_research_gaps: The literature provides a clear pathway for low-cost classroom thermal monitoring: use reliable T/RH sensors, install them carefully, log continuously, and combine room-level metrics with metadata and occupant feedback. The main gaps are more classroom studies with full comfort instrumentation, better validation of simplified alert rules against formal standards, and stronger longitudinal evidence that sensor-driven interventions improve thermal equity, learning conditions, and resilience under extreme heat.
